newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia seen crying foul over environment aims.
newsitem.headline: Asia seen crying foul over environment aims.

text.p: Singapore, the Asian member of a group of nations pushing a package of initiatives to guard the environment, may face resistance within the region to its targets, experts and officials said on Wednesday.
This week Singapore joined Germany, Brazil and South Africa to promote new measures for sustainable development and environmental protection at the United Nations Earth Summit.

The four called on the summit to send a "clear message" on greenhouse gas emissions that affect climate change. Among other steps, they asked for 15 percent reductions in emissions below 1990 levels by 2010, with a 10 percent reduction by 2005.

Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong, saying Singapore was between the developed and developing worlds, noted the latter's suspicions richer nations were using environmental issues as disguised protectionism.
"Developing countries deem it unreasonable that they are required to address long-term environmental problems at the expense of immediate needs," he told the summit.
He termed the group of four's proposals a modest initiative addressing the needs of both developing and developed countries, saying all needed to move ahead.
"Environmental interdependence is a stark and inescapable reality. We have no illusions about the necessity for a concerted and continuing effort."

But some say Singapore's pro-environment stance is a luxury it enjoys by virtue of its First World wealth and booming economy, centred on high tech exports and position as a financial and services hub. "Singapore can sit on that council and not look like a hypocrite, of all countries in the region," said analyst Bruce Gale of the Political & Economic Risk Consultancy (PERC).
He said urban Singapore had enforced strict standards itself but he doubted it could use moral or diplomatic persuasion to convince others they should fall readily in line.

China has made environmental protection one of its most high-profile policies as its economic boom causes pollution to soar, but it remains wary of attempts by rich nations to focus on rising emissions in the developing world.
Economically developed nations pumped out far more greenhouse gases per head of population than China, said one official of its National Environmental Protection Agency.
"As a developing country, China will not shoulder responsibility of greenhouse gas emissions, and over-consumption of energy," he said.
India has balked at committing itself to a specific reduction of gasses and focused on pressing rich nations to live up to environmental commitments they have already made.

Environment Minister Saifuddin Soz told the Earth Summit on Tuesday that India was deeply concerned there was an effort by rich nations "to prescribe equal obligations and liabilities on unequal players".
Jun Min-yung, an official at the Energy and Resources Policy Division at the South Korean Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy, said demands on developing nations were unfair.

"Advanced nations have been emitting gasses for 200 years since the Industrial Revolution compared to South Korea's 20 year history of industrialisation. We cannot reduce the levels until our economy is stable and it will take at least 30 years for our economy to reach the level of advanced nations."

Emmy Hafield, director of the Indonesian Environmental Forum (Walhi), said the reduction of greenhouse gas cannot be done in a short time. "The world's greatest emitter is the United States and that country has not shown any commitment yet," she said.

Further south, Australia, the world's largest coal exporter, has fought hard Prime Minister John Howard, under fire from environmentalists for snubbing the New York summit, argues across-the-board targets would hammer Australian industry, throw thousands of people out of work as the country battles chronic unemployment, and shave 1.5 percent off gross domestic product.
He has vigorously pushed Australia's campaign for individually-tailored targets in talks with world leaders.

Japan has also stopped short of setting a numerical target for reducing greenhouse gases and instead proposed "medium-term" measures such as pooling environment aid and transferring environment-related technology to developing countries.
One environmentalist said Singapore should bring industry leaders into the process to build regional support.

"Singapore has to expand into the region for industry leaders, the educational process, to bring it to the level of consciousness that is starting to take root here," said Peyton Coffin, chairman of Singapore's Preserve Planet Earth Committee.
